### Giovanni Antonio Grassi (1775–1849)

- **Born**: August 2, 1775, in Lugano, Swiss Confederation (now Switzerland)
- **Died**: December 23, 1849, in Stonyhurst, England
- **Nationality**: Italian-Swiss (Ticinese)
- **Religious Order**: Society of Jesus (Jesuit)
- **Occupation**: Priest, educator, astronomer, academic administrator

#### Background and Early Life
Grassi entered the Jesuit order in 1792. Due to the suppression of the Jesuits in many European countries, he continued his studies and formation in Russia, where the order had been allowed to survive under the protection of Empress Catherine the Great.

#### Scientific and Academic Career
- Grassi was trained in mathematics, physics, and astronomy.
- He taught at the Jesuit College in Polotsk (in modern-day Belarus), where he conducted astronomical observations and helped build an observatory.

#### Georgetown College (1812–1825)
- In 1812, Grassi was sent to the United States to serve as the Vice Prefect of the Maryland Mission of the Jesuits.
- He became President of Georgetown College (now Georgetown University) in Washington, D.C.
- During his tenure, he expanded the curriculum, strengthened academic standards, and oversaw the construction of new buildings, including a scientific laboratory and an observatory.
- He personally taught subjects such as mathematics and astronomy.
- Grassi played a key role in transforming Georgetown into a more structured academic institution.

#### Return to Europe
- In 1825, he returned to Europe due to conflicts with other Jesuit superiors and tensions over governance.
- He served in various Jesuit colleges in Italy and later settled at Stonyhurst College in England, a Jesuit-run institution, where he spent his final years in teaching and religious work.

#### Scientific Contributions
- Grassi was known for his interest in meteorology and astronomy.
- He corresponded with other scientists of his time and maintained detailed meteorological records.

#### Legacy
- A lunar crater, **Grassi**, is named after him in recognition of his contributions to astronomy.
- He is remembered as an influential early leader in American Catholic education.
